PCG_DistanceFromGeometry.summary: Writes each point's distance to a reference geometry: to its surface, its edges, or its nearest point.
PCG_DistanceFromGeometry.description:
For every selected point the node finds the closest location on the reference geometry (second input) and writes the straight-line distance to a point attribute (`dist` by default).

*Surface* measures to the reference's polygons, *Edges* to its polygon edges and polylines (use it for curve networks), *Points* to its nearest point. With *Max Distance* on, farther points get the max value and the search stops there, which makes large inputs much faster.

The optional mask converts distance into a 0..1 falloff through a ramp, ready to drive colour, displacement or scattering density.

inputs.reference: Geometry the distance is measured to.

outputs.geo: The input with the distance (and mask) attribute.
outputs.report: Point count, metric and the distance range.

params.group: Only these points get a distance; the others keep 0 (or their existing value).
params.reference_group: Primitives (Surface, Edges) or points (Points) of the reference to measure to. Empty means all.
params.metric: What on the reference counts: Surface (closest point on polygons), Edges (closest point on edges / curves) or Points (nearest point).
params.distance_attribute: Point attribute the distance is written to.
params.max_distance: Largest distance written; farther points get this value. Also limits the search radius.
params.output_mask: Also write a 0..1 mask: distance divided by Mask Radius, looked up in Mask Ramp.
params.mask_attribute: Point attribute the mask is written to.
params.mask_radius: Distance at which the ramp reaches its right end; farther points get the ramp's last value.
params.mask_ramp: Ramp as position:value pairs over distance / Mask Radius. The default fades from 1 at the reference to 0 at Mask Radius.

PCG_DistanceAlongGeometry.summary: Distance from start points measured along the surface (geodesic or along edges).
PCG_DistanceAlongGeometry.description:
Measures how far every point is from the start points when travelling **on** the geometry, not through space: the distance around a sphere, along a winding road mesh, across a character's skin.

*Geodesic* uses the heat method: it diffuses heat from the start points for a short time, normalises the heat gradient and solves for a distance with that gradient. The result follows the surface smoothly. *Edges* finds the shortest path along edges; it is exact along edges but overestimates diagonals across faces (up to 41% across a quad grid).

Points not connected to any start point get -1.

outputs.geo: The input with the distance (and mask) attribute.
outputs.report: Sources, method, unreachable points and the largest distance.

params.start_points: Point group or numbers the distance is measured from.
params.method: Geodesic (heat method: smooth, follows the surface) or Edges (shortest path along edges).
params.heat_time: Diffusion time of the heat method, in mean edge lengths squared. Larger values are smoother but less exact.
params.distance_attribute: Point attribute the distance is written to.
params.max_distance: Largest distance written; farther points get this value.
params.output_mask: Also write a 0..1 mask: distance divided by Mask Radius, looked up in Mask Ramp.
params.mask_attribute: Point attribute the mask is written to.
params.mask_radius: Distance at which the ramp reaches its right end; farther points get the ramp's last value.
params.mask_ramp: Ramp as position:value pairs over distance / Mask Radius. The default fades from 1 at the reference to 0 at Mask Radius.

PCG_PathDeform.description:
Lays one axis of the input (Deform Axis, +Z by default) along the curve in the second input: the coordinate on that axis becomes a distance along the curve, the other two coordinates become offsets in the curve's frame there. Frames are rotation-minimising, so long shapes don't twist unless Roll or Twist ask for it.

With *Stretch to Curve* the input's length along the axis is fitted to the curve; without it the axis coordinate is used as arc length directly (times Scale). Offset slides the shape along the curve. Past the curve's ends the shape continues straight along the end tangent.

A coarse curve gives a faceted bend; resample it for smooth results.

inputs.curve: Curve to follow (the first curve primitive).

outputs.report: Point count, curve length and points beyond the curve's ends.

params.curve_group: Which curve primitive of the second input to follow; the first one in the group is used.
params.deform_axis: Axis of the input that is laid along the curve.
params.stretch_to_curve: Fit the input's extent along the deform axis to the whole curve.
params.offset: Slide along the curve, in world units (or a fraction of the curve length).
params.offset_as_fraction: Read Offset as a fraction of the curve length.
params.cross_scale: Scale of the two cross-section axes.
params.roll: Rotate the shape about the curve, in degrees.
params.twist: Extra rotation that grows to this many degrees at the curve's end.
params.up_mode: Minimal Rotation (the frame is carried along without twisting) or Constant (each frame faces the Up vector).
params.up_x: Up vector: the start of the frame (Minimal Rotation) or the direction every frame faces (Constant).

PCG_PolyWire.summary: Builds tubes along every edge of a curve network, with closed joints at branches.
PCG_PolyWire.description:
Puts a tube on every edge of the input's polylines and polygons. Unlike Sweep, which works one curve at a time, PolyWire treats the edges as a network: shared points are joined, so branching structures (trees, L-systems, wire frames, road graphs) come out as one connected set of tubes.

The network is cut into chains at ends and junctions; each chain gets a tube with rotation-minimising frames. Junctions and sharp bends get a sphere of the wire radius so branches have no gaps, and open ends get round or flat caps. The radius can come from point attributes (`width` as a diameter, `pscale` as a radius).

inputs.geo: Curves and / or polygons whose edges get wires.

outputs.report: Chains, joints and the size of the result.

params.radius: Tube radius when Radius From is Wire Radius.
params.radius_from: Constant Wire Radius, or per point from `width` (diameter) or `pscale` (radius).
params.divisions: Number of sides around each tube.
params.end_caps: How open ends are closed: Round (half sphere), Flat (a polygon) or not at all.
params.joints: Add spheres at junctions and sharp bends so the tubes meet without gaps.
params.joint_angle: Bends sharper than this (in degrees) inside a chain also get a sphere.
params.carry_attributes: Copy the curve's point attributes (such as Cd) to the tube points made from each curve point.

PCG_Thicken.summary: Gives open surfaces a thickness with a second skin and side walls.
PCG_Thicken.description:
Turns a single-sided surface (a leaf, a cloth panel, a terrain patch) into a solid: a second skin is made Thickness away along the point normals and the borders are closed with side walls.

*Side* chooses where the thickness goes: *Outward* keeps the input as the inner skin, *Inward* as the outer skin, *Both* makes the input the mid-surface. Front, back and side faces are put into groups. Closed meshes become hollow shells. Thickness is measured along point normals, so sharp convex corners come out a little thinner, as with any normal offset.

params.side: Where the thickness goes: both sides (centered), outward or inward.
params.divisions: Number of edge loops across the side walls.
params.front_group: Primitive group for the faces moved along the normals.
params.back_group: Primitive group for the faces on the other side.
params.side_group: Primitive group for the side walls.

PCG_CurveFillet.summary: Rounds polyline corners with circular arcs.
PCG_CurveFillet.description:
Replaces the selected corners of polylines with circular arcs of the given radius, tangent to both neighbouring segments. With *Limit Radius* the arc shrinks where a segment is too short to fit it, so neighbouring fillets never overlap.

Closed polylines and polygons have every point treated as a corner; open curves keep their end points. Nearly straight corners are left alone. The arc points copy the corner's point attributes.

outputs.report: Number of corners rounded and the new point count.

params.points: Corner points to round. Empty means all corners.
params.limit_radius: Shrink the arc where the neighbouring segments are shorter than the arc needs.
params.include_closed: Also round closed polylines and polygons.

PCG_Pack.summary: Packs pieces of geometry into packed primitives: one point per piece.
PCG_Pack.description:
Turns every piece of the input into a packed primitive: a single point that carries the whole piece. Pieces are defined by a piece attribute (such as `name`), by connectivity, or the whole input is one piece. The piece's pivot (centroid, bounding box center, bottom center or origin) becomes the packed point.

Packed geometry is cheap to transform, merge and copy, and the viewport draws it as GPU instances. Nodes that need real polygons unpack it automatically, so a packed input never gives a wrong result.

params.pack_by: How pieces are found: by Piece Attribute, by Connectivity, or Everything as one piece.
params.piece_attribute: Primitives sharing a value of this attribute form one piece.
params.pivot: Where the packed point of each piece goes: centroid, bounding box center, origin or bottom center.

PCG_Unpack.summary: Expands packed primitives back into real geometry.
PCG_Unpack.description:
Replaces packed primitives with the geometry they carry, transformed to where they are; other primitives pass through. Copies made by Copy to Points with *Pack and Instance* unpack to exactly what Copy to Points gives without packing, attributes included.

*Transfer Attributes* copies attributes of the packed points and primitives (such as a colour set after packing) onto the unpacked pieces.

outputs.report: Packed primitives unpacked and distinct pieces.

params.transfer_attributes: Attributes of the packed points / primitives copied onto the unpacked points / primitives (patterns allowed).

PCG_Assemble.summary: Names the connected pieces of a mesh piece0, piece1 ... and optionally packs each piece.
PCG_Assemble.description:
Finds the connected pieces among the group's primitives (primitives sharing points belong together) and writes Output Prefix plus the piece number into a string primitive attribute, numbered in order of each piece's first primitive. This is the usual step after a fracture or a Boolean that leaves loose parts.

With **Create Packed Geometry** every piece becomes a packed primitive placed at its pivot, ready to be moved per piece, instanced in the viewport or exported with GPU instancing. Primitives outside the group pass through unchanged.

outputs.report: Number of pieces and of packed primitives.

params.group: Primitives to assemble; the rest pass through.
params.name_attribute: String primitive attribute that receives the piece names.
params.create_packed: Turn every piece into a packed primitive.
params.pivot: Where each packed piece's point goes: centroid, bounding box center, origin or bottom center.

PCG_Assemble.houdini_notes: Counterpart of the Assemble SOP. Connectivity is by shared points; there is no separate Connectivity Attribute, and the packed fragments carry no path attribute.

PCG_LotSubdivision.summary: Cuts polygons such as city blocks into lots by repeated straight cuts.
PCG_LotSubdivision.description:
Every selected polygon is cut in two by a straight line, each half is cut again, and so on for `Iterations` passes: one pass gives 2 lots, two give 4, three give 8. A lot whose area is below `Minimum Lot Size` is left as it is, so large blocks end up with more lots than small ones.

`Alignment` decides the direction of the cuts. *Bounding Box* cuts across the longer side of the lot's bounding box, so all cuts are parallel to the axes - right for a regular grid of streets. *Longest Edge* cuts perpendicular to the lot's longest edge, so the cuts follow a slanted or irregular block. `Irregularity` moves each cut away from the middle, which gives lots of different sizes.

With `Cluster Lots` on, neighbouring lots of the same block (lots sharing an edge) are joined until `Number of Clusters` remain: the shared edges disappear and the outline stays, giving L-shaped and irregular parcels.

The polygons can be concave, but must be planar and must not intersect themselves. The lots share points along common edges, including where one lot's corner meets the middle of its neighbour's side. Each lot gets the prim attributes `lot` (its number), `block` (the source polygon) and `area`, and the source polygon's own prim attributes. Feed the result to Building Generator (PCG).

outputs.geo: One polygon per lot; polygons outside the group pass through.
outputs.report: Number of lots and blocks, and the smallest and largest lot area.

params.group: Polygons to cut. Empty means all; the others pass through unchanged.
params.alignment: Direction of the cuts: Bounding Box (parallel to the axes of the polygon's plane - world X and Z for a horizontal block) or Longest Edge (perpendicular to the lot's longest edge).
params.min_lot_size: Lots with an area below this are not cut further.
params.iterations: Number of cutting passes. Each pass cuts every lot in two.
params.rand_seed: Seed of the random cut positions (used when Irregularity is above 0).
params.irregularity: 0 cuts every lot through the middle. Higher values move each cut randomly, up to anywhere in the middle 80% at 1.
params.cluster_lots: Joins neighbouring lots into larger parcels.
params.clusters: Number of parcels left per block after joining.
params.cluster_seed: Seed of the random choice of which neighbours are joined.

PCG_LotSubdivision.houdini_notes: Corresponds to SideFX Labs Lot Subdivision 2.0 with the same parameters. The exact cut positions and the clustering order are the plugin's own, so the same seed does not give the same lots as Houdini.

PCG_BuildingGenerator.summary: Turns footprint polygons into buildings with floors, facade modules, ledges and a roof.
PCG_BuildingGenerator.description:
Every footprint polygon (taken as seen from above; up is +Y, the base is the footprint's lowest point) becomes one building. Its walls are split into floors of `Full Floor Height`, and each floor of each wall into bays of about `Module Width`; the bays are stretched evenly so they fill the wall exactly. Each bay holds one module.

**Modules and patterns.** `Facade Module Pattern` is a list of module names separated by spaces, repeated along the wall as seen from outside, left to right: `window window door`. Writing `a|b|c` picks one of the alternatives at random per bay. Five modules are built in: `wall` (blank), `window`, `door`, `shopfront` (a wide, low window) and `balcony` (a glazed door with a slab and a railing standing 0.9 m out; parts `balcony` and `railing`); their openings are recessed by `Inset`. If a module library is connected to the `modules` input, a name found there is used instead. A library is ordinary geometry whose prims carry a string attribute `name`; all prims with one name form one module. The module's width (x) and height (y) are fitted to the bay, z = 0 is the wall plane and +z points out of the building, so a balcony can stick out and a window can be recessed. A prim attribute `part` on the library is kept.

**Corners, ledges, roof.** With `Corners` on, a strip at both ends of every wall is a pilaster, or the convex / concave corner module from the library. `Top` and `Bottom` add an extruded band along the top or the foot of every floor, mitred round the corners. The roof is flat, flat inside a parapet, or -- over a four-cornered footprint -- a gable or hip roof: the ridge runs along the longer sides at `Roof Pitch`, the eaves stand out by `Roof Overhang`, and a gable's end triangles are walls. `Roof Attribute` picks the roof per footprint from a string prim attribute.

**Front.** With a `Front Pattern` and a vector prim attribute on the footprint (`Front Attribute`, the direction toward the street), the wall facing that way gets the front pattern on its ground floor: doors and shopfronts face the street, the other walls keep the facade pattern.

**Setback.** `Footprint Inset` moves the walls in from the footprint, so lots that touch each other leave streets and yards between the buildings; a footprint too small for it is left empty.

**Plinth.** `Foundation Depth` extends the walls below the base as a plain band (part `plinth`, floor -2), so a building standing on uneven ground shows no gap underneath.

**Number of floors.** Per footprint: its `Height Attribute` (metres, divided by the floor height) if present, otherwise its `Floors Attribute`, otherwise a random number between `Floors Min` and `Floors Max`.

**Floor overrides.** One line per floor, for example `0: height=4.5 pattern=door shopfront shopfront` for a taller ground floor with shops. `0` is the ground floor, `-1` the top floor; `height` and `pattern` are both optional.

The output carries the prim attributes `building`, `floor` (-1 on the roof, -2 on the plinth), `part` and `material` (wall, glass, frame, door, corner, ledge, roof, parapet, plinth, or the library's parts), `module`, the footprint's own prim attributes (a lot number, a town name), a prim group per part, a colour `Cd`, and vertex `uv` in metres (u along the wall, v up) so tiling textures keep their scale.

**Street fronts, chimneys, yard walls.** `Front Pattern Attribute` names a string prim attribute holding a front pattern per footprint (shopfronts in a town's core, a door elsewhere); empty values use `Front Pattern`. `Chimney Chance` is the probability, seeded per building, of a chimney stack on a gable or hip roof, just off the ridge (part `chimney`). `Yard Wall Height` above 0 builds a wall `Yard Wall Thickness` thick along the footprint's own outline -- the lot line, outside the setback -- on every side but the front one (part `yardwall`, floor -3), so lots read as yards. `Notch Attribute` names a float prim attribute (0..0.8): that fraction of the depth and the width is cut out of the back corner of a four-cornered footprint (opposite the front), making an L-shaped building; with a gable or hip roof it gets two gable wings, a cross gable: the front wing over the full width, the back wing running from the front ridge to its own gable over the back wall, no higher than the front ridge. `Side Front Attribute` names a vector prim attribute holding a corner lot's second street: the wall facing it gets the front's ground floor too (the same front pattern), so a corner building faces both streets.

inputs.geo: Footprint polygons, for example the lots of Lot Subdivision (PCG).
inputs.modules: Optional module library: geometry with a string prim attribute `name`.

outputs.report: Number of buildings, floors and faces, and the face count per part.

params.group: Footprints to build on. Empty means all.
params.color_floors: Colours every floor differently, to check the floor layout, instead of colouring by part.
params.floors_min: Smallest random number of floors, used when the footprint has neither attribute.
params.floors_attribute: Prim attribute on the footprints that gives the number of floors.
params.height_attribute: Prim attribute on the footprints that gives the building height in metres. Takes precedence over the floors attribute.
params.rand_seed: Seed of the random floor counts, module alternatives and wall tints.
params.facade_pattern: Module names along the wall, separated by spaces and repeated. `a|b` picks one at random per bay. Built in: `wall`, `window`, `door`, `shopfront`.
params.module_width: Target width of a bay. The number of bays is the wall length divided by this, rounded; the bays then stretch to fit.
params.window_width: Width of the built-in window as a fraction of the bay.
params.window_height: Height of the built-in window as a fraction of the floor height.
params.window_sill: Height of the wall below the built-in window, as a fraction of the floor height.
params.inset: Depth by which the built-in openings are recessed.
params.corners: Adds a corner strip at both ends of every wall (skipped on walls shorter than 2.5 corner widths).
params.convex_corner_module: Library module for corners that point outwards. Empty gives a plain pilaster.
params.concave_corner_module: Library module for corners that point inwards. Empty gives a plain pilaster.
params.top_ledge: Adds a ledge along the top of every floor.
params.bottom_ledge: Adds a ledge along the foot of every floor.
params.ledge_depth: How far the ledges stand out from the wall.
params.roof: Flat, flat inside a parapet, gable or hip. Gable and hip need a four-cornered footprint; others get a flat roof.
params.parapet_height: Height of the parapet above the roof.
params.floor_overrides: One line per overridden floor: `index: height=H pattern=...`. Index 0 is the ground floor, -1 the top floor.
params.footprint_inset: Moves the walls in from the footprint by this distance, so lots that touch each other leave streets and yards between the buildings. A footprint too small for the setback gets no building.
params.foundation_depth: Adds a plain band of wall this deep below the base (part `plinth`), so a building on uneven ground shows no gap under its walls.
params.front_attribute: Vector prim attribute on the footprints giving the direction their front faces (toward the street). The wall whose outward normal is nearest to it is the front.
params.front_pattern: Ground-floor module pattern of the front wall, so doors and shopfronts face the street. Empty turns it off. A front wall with fewer bays than the pattern shows the pattern's middle (one bay of `window door window` is the door).
params.roof_pitch: Slope of gable and hip roofs in degrees.
params.roof_overhang: How far the eaves of gable and hip roofs stand out from the walls.
params.roof_attribute: Optional string prim attribute on the footprints that picks the roof per building (`flat`, `parapet`, `gable` or `hip`; empty values use the Roof menu).
params.front_pattern_attribute: Optional string prim attribute on the footprints: their own front pattern (empty values use Front Pattern). Needs Front Attribute.
params.chimney_chance: Probability (0..1, seeded per building) of a chimney on a gable or hip roof.
params.yard_wall_height: Height of a wall along the footprint outline on every side but the front (0 = no wall). Sits 0.3 m into the ground.
params.yard_wall_thickness: Thickness of the yard walls, built inside the footprint outline.
params.notch_attribute: Optional float prim attribute (0..0.8): the share of the depth and the width cut out of the back corner of a four-cornered footprint -- an L-shaped building (two gable wings under a gable or hip roof).
params.side_front_attribute: Optional vector prim attribute: the direction of a corner lot's second street (0 0 0 = none). The wall facing it gets the front pattern on the ground floor too.

PCG_BuildingGenerator.houdini_notes: Corresponds to SideFX Labs Building Generator 4.0: floors, facade module pattern, corner modules, top and bottom ledges and floor overrides. Differences: the input is footprints rather than building volumes; ledges are always the simple extruded kind (Houdini's Simple Ledges); bays stretch to fill the wall, so there is no sideslop module; the built-in modules, the roofs (flat, parapet, gable, hip) and the front pattern are additions, so the node works without a library.

PCG_LODCreate.summary: Builds a chain of levels of detail from a mesh, optionally ending in impostor cards.
PCG_LODCreate.description:
`Percent Triangles` lists one value per level. A level at 100 is the mesh as it is; every other level is reduced from the original to that share of its triangles by quadric edge collapse (the method of Poly Reduce (PCG)). `Threshold Distance` gives the camera distance at which each level starts; left empty, the levels start at 0 and then at `First Distance`, doubling each time.

With `Preserve UVs` on, UV seams are kept in place, so every level can use the textures baked for LOD0. `Recalculate Normals` writes new vertex normals on the reduced levels, split at edges sharper than `Cusp Angle`. `Last LOD is Impostor` replaces the last level by two crossed upright cards the size of the bounding box, with uv 0-1 each, ready for an atlas from Impostor Textures (PCG).

**Custom meshes.** A model made another way can replace a level: connect it to `custom` with an integer prim attribute `lod` on its faces (and `name`, to match an asset). The level's percent then applies to it, 100 keeping it as it is. This is the way for meshes that reduction would tear -- a building's facade full of openings, say, replaced at a distance by its massing.

If the mesh has a string prim attribute `name`, every name is treated as one asset and gets its own chain.

All levels come out in one geometry. Each prim carries `lod` (the level), `part` (`LOD0`, `LOD1`, ...), `name` (`<asset>_LOD0`, or `LOD0` without asset names), `lod_distance` and `impostor`; there is a prim group per level. Export Mesh (PCG) writes one node per `name`, which is how engines pick up LOD chains.

inputs.geo: Mesh to make levels of detail for.
inputs.custom: Optional custom meshes: faces with an integer prim attribute `lod` replace that level (matched to the asset by `name`, if any).

outputs.geo: All levels (or the chosen one) in one geometry.
outputs.report: Triangle count, distance and impostor flag of every level.

params.percents: Triangle share of every level in percent of the original, separated by spaces. The number of values is the number of levels.
params.distances: Distance at which each level starts, one value per level. Empty computes them from First Distance.
params.first_distance: Start distance of LOD1 when Threshold Distance is empty; later levels double it.
params.last_lod_impostor: Replaces the last level by two crossed cards.
params.preserve_uvs: Keeps UV seams fixed during reduction so all levels share one texture set.
params.boundary_weight: How strongly open borders are kept in place during reduction.
params.recalculate_normals: Writes vertex normals on the reduced levels.
params.cusp_angle: Edges sharper than this angle stay hard when normals are recalculated.
params.name_prefix: Prefix of the level names in the `name` attribute.
params.view: All: every level in place (select one downstream by its group). Single LOD: only the level chosen below. Debug All LOD: all levels side by side.
params.level: Level shown in Single LOD mode.
params.spacing: Distance between levels in Debug All LOD mode, in widths of the mesh.

PCG_LODCreate.houdini_notes: Corresponds to SideFX Labs LOD Create 2.0: LOD count, Percent Triangles, Threshold Distance, Custom Mesh (as a second input), Last LOD is Impostor, Recalculate Normals with Cusp Angle, the mesh name prefix and the viewing modes. Not included: FBX export and texture baking (use Export Mesh and COP Bake Textures), shader consolidation, Remove Insides, Preserve Quads (the reduced levels are triangles) and the camera-driven viewing mode.

PCG_ImpostorTextures.summary: Renders an object from a grid of directions into an impostor atlas, and outputs the card to show it on.
PCG_ImpostorTextures.description:
An impostor replaces a distant object by a single card that shows a picture of the object from roughly the right direction. This node renders those pictures: every frame is an orthographic view of the whole object, framed on its bounding sphere so all frames have the same scale, and the frames are packed into one atlas.

`Impostor Type` chooses the directions:

- **Octahedron**: `XY Frames` x `XY Frames` directions over the whole sphere, laid out by the octahedral map. Neighbouring frames are neighbouring directions, so an engine can blend between them.
- **Hemi-Octahedron**: the same over the upper half only - for trees and buildings, which are never seen from below, this doubles the angular resolution.
- **Fixed Axis**: all frames go round the up axis at one `Elevation` - for billboards that only turn about Y.
- **3D**: `XY Frames` azimuths by `XY Frames (Y)` elevations, a latitude / longitude grid.

The atlas has the layers `C` (linear base colour from the geometry's `Cd`, which is a display colour and is decoded; unlit), `alpha`, `N` (the normal, in world or view space, signed), `depth` (0-1 across the bounding sphere along the view direction; 0.5 is the plane through the centre) and `beauty` (the base colour lit by a fixed sun, for engines that use a pre-lit atlas). Frame (0, 0) is the lower-left sprite. Write the layers out with COP Write File (PCG).

The `card` output is a quad the size of the bounding sphere, centred on the object, with uv 0-1 and the detail attributes `impostor_type`, `frames_x`, `frames_y`, `radius` and `center`.

inputs.geo: Object to make the impostor of.

outputs.cop: The atlas (layers C, alpha, N, depth, beauty).
outputs.card: The impostor card with the settings as detail attributes.
outputs.report: Type, frame counts, atlas size, bounding radius and centre.

params.impostor_type: Arrangement of the view directions: Octahedron, Hemi-Octahedron, Fixed Axis or 3D.
params.sprite_resolution: Size of one frame in pixels. The atlas is the frame count times this.
params.frames_x: Number of frames across and up. The octahedron types use the first value for both.
params.elevation: Camera elevation in degrees for Fixed Axis.
params.zoom: Above 1 zooms in on the object (cropping the bounding sphere) to use more of each frame.
params.normal_space: World space, or view space (x right, y up, z toward the camera).
params.sun_direction: Direction toward the sun for the beauty layer (X Y Z).

PCG_ImpostorTextures.houdini_notes: Corresponds to SideFX Labs Impostor Texture (and its successor Impostor Baker): Octahedron, 3D and Fixed Axis types, Sprite Resolution, XY Frames, Octahedron Zoom, and the base colour, normal and beauty atlases. The Animation type is not included. The colour comes from the `Cd` attribute; textured materials are not rendered. Octahedron frames sample the map at both ends of its range, the convention game engines use for blending.

PCG_WorldManifest.summary: Writes World.json, one file describing an exported world, plus one manifest per streaming tile.
PCG_WorldManifest.description:
An engine import should not have to know how a world's files are named. This node reads back everything the export nodes wrote under **Folder** and writes `World.json` beside them, with one `tiles/Tile_x{i}_y{j}.json` per tile, so an import script reads a single file.

What it recognises, by content rather than by name:

- **Image sets**: every sidecar JSON of COP Write File (height, colour, normal, splat maps, layer textures ...) with its channels, bit depth, decode rule, size and files. A set tiled on the same grid as the world lists its file in each tile. The height map (the set in the `height` folder) also becomes the `terrain` section: range in metres, samples, metres per sample, shared edges.
- **Instance tables**: Export Instances' index and its CSVs. Every row is counted per asset and per tile.
- **Meshes**: every glb with its nodes, meshes, materials, triangle counts and bounds (POSITION min / max with the node's translation and scale; a GPU-instanced node lists its instance count). A `.lods.json` beside it (Export Mesh's LOD Manifest) adds each asset's LOD nodes and switch distances, and LOD assets are placed in the tile of their bounds' centre. Other meshes with bounds (water, say) are listed in every tile they overlap. The `assets` folder is treated as a library and not placed.
- **Polylines**: OBJ `l` records (roads), with their count, length and bounds; each tile gets the length of each set inside it.
- Everything else is listed under `files`.

The role of a file is its first folder under Folder (height, texture, instances, buildings, roads, water, assets ...). `coordinates` states the convention: metres, +Y up, x east and z south, where (0, 0) lies (**Origin**), the tile grid (**Tile Size**; tile (i, j) covers x from i × tile), the image orientation (row 0 at the tile's smallest z) and how Unreal and Unity map the axes. A tile's `bounds` joins the terrain's decoded height range over its extent with the instances, buildings and roads in it.

The manifest only sees files that exist when it runs: link the exports' outputs (Export Mesh's path, Export Instances' and COP Write File's reports) to the `after` inputs, and they run first. The inputs take any type, so the image of a render that comes last can be linked too: ComfyUI runs an export as soon as its input is ready, so everything that render read has been written by then. **Extra JSON** (an object) adds keys of your own, such as road classes with their widths and materials; it cannot replace format, version, coordinates or tiles.

inputs.after1: Optional, any type: an export's path or report, or a render's image. Only used to make those nodes (and everything they read) run before the manifest; likewise after2 to after8.
inputs.after2: Optional, any type: like after1, another output that must run before the manifest.
inputs.after3: Optional, any type: like after1, another output that must run before the manifest.
inputs.after4: Optional, any type: like after1, another output that must run before the manifest.
inputs.after5: Optional, any type: like after1, another output that must run before the manifest.
inputs.after6: Optional, any type: like after1, another output that must run before the manifest.
inputs.after7: Optional, any type: like after1, another output that must run before the manifest.
inputs.after8: Optional, any type: like after1, another output that must run before the manifest.

outputs.path: World.json's path, relative to the output folder.
outputs.report: JSON counts: tiles, image sets, meshes, polylines, instances, other files.

params.folder: The world's folder under ComfyUI's output folder.
params.world_size: Edge of the square world in metres.
params.tile_size: Edge of a streaming tile in metres, the grid of the _x{i}_y{j} files.
params.origin: Where (0, 0) lies: the north-west corner (the world spans 0 to World Size) or the centre (minus half to plus half).
params.extra_json: A JSON object whose keys are added to World.json (for example road classes). Empty adds nothing.

PCG_WorldManifest.houdini_notes: No Houdini node; in a Houdini pipeline this is the job of a PDG / Python step after the ROPs, collecting their outputs into a level description.
